KV cache.simple: Imagine the model reading a long conversation. It keeps reusable attention calculations for earlier tokens instead of calculating all of them again at every next word.
KV cache.technical: During autoregressive decoding, transformer layers cache previously computed attention keys and values. New generated tokens add K/V entries, avoiding recomputation over prefix tokens. KV caching primarily speeds decoding; prompt prefill still processes new input. Cache footprint grows with layers, heads and sequence length, and reuse depends on the inference server/session.
KV cache.example: After the first generated token, the second token can attend to cached previous token representations.
KV cache.project: For a voice assistant, persistent conversation context can raise latency; monitor prompt prefill, decode, memory usage and KV-cache eviction separately.
KV cache.answer: KV cache stores attention key/value tensors from earlier tokens so the model can decode the next token without recomputing the entire prefix. It reduces generation cost, but does not eliminate first-token prefill time. Long prompts, cold workers or cache eviction may still make first replies slow.
workflow: New prompt → prefill K/V for prompt tokens
Decode one token → append its K/V
Repeat token generation with cached history
Invalidate/evict on incompatible context or resource pressure
mistakes: Confusing KV cache with semantic response caching
Claiming it removes retrieval or prefill latency
Assuming it survives every unrelated request
followups: How does prefix caching differ?
What happens when context length grows?

Chunking & overlap.simple: Split a large policy into manageable passages so search can retrieve just the relevant part.
Chunking & overlap.technical: Chunking determines retrieval granularity. Tune token size and overlap to document structure, embedding limits, recall, precision and answer context budget. Preserve section headers, page references, ACLs and source IDs. Overlap can protect boundary context but causes redundancy and higher index/storage costs.
Chunking & overlap.example: A 40-page credit-card policy can be divided by headings into coherent 300–600 token sections rather than embedding all 40 pages as one vector.
Chunking & overlap.project: In the banking voice assistant, retrieved FAQ or policy chunks should keep product, tenant and version metadata; otherwise a correct-looking clause can come from the wrong bank policy.
Chunking & overlap.answer: We chunk documents because a single large embedding loses topical precision and a full policy may exceed prompt budgets. I split by semantic sections with measured overlap, attach metadata and evaluate retrieval on a golden set. The chunk size is tuned using recall, precision and latency rather than a fixed guess.
workflow: Split at semantic boundaries, optionally overlap
Retrieve and evaluate on held-out questions
mistakes: Using arbitrary character slicing across tables
Treating overlap as always beneficial
Dropping ACL and version fields
followups: Does user query get chunked?
How do you handle tables?

Incremental RAG ingestion.simple: Update only the documents that changed rather than rebuilding the whole search index every day.
Incremental RAG ingestion.technical: Track document IDs, content checksums, version IDs, timestamps and deletions. A change triggers reparse, rechunk and reembedding for affected material; stale chunk IDs are tombstoned, index updates are idempotent, and retrieval uses an atomic version/active flag to avoid mixed policy versions.
Incremental RAG ingestion.example: If policy 42 is revised, replace its old vector chunks and metadata; other 9,999 policies remain unchanged.
Incremental RAG ingestion.project: For updated banking policies, a checksum/event pipeline can process the changed document, switch active version only after validation, and quarantine failed ingestions.
Incremental RAG ingestion.answer: Incremental RAG ingestion tracks changed or deleted source documents, regenerates their chunks and embeddings, and retires stale index entries. Unlike incremental data engineering loads, we must manage embeddings, document versions and retrieval correctness—not merely load new rows.
workflow: Detect change/delete with event, checksum or CDC
Atomically activate version and remove stale references
mistakes: Only appending new vectors and leaving stale policy chunks
Ignoring source deletes
Making unvalidated content immediately searchable
followups: How do you avoid old and new policies mixing?
What if embedding dimensions changed?

Graph RAG vs standard RAG.simple: Normal RAG retrieves relevant passages; Graph RAG can also follow relationships between people, rules, entities and events.
Graph RAG vs standard RAG.technical: Graph RAG builds or queries entity and relationship structures alongside document retrieval. It helps multi-hop questions and relationship reasoning, but requires entity extraction, graph maintenance, permission-aware traversal and extra latency. Hybrid vector+graph retrieval is often more practical than replacing vector RAG.
Graph RAG vs standard RAG.example: For “Which supplier change affected delayed refinery shipments?”, graph edges between purchase order, supplier, site and delay are valuable.
Graph RAG vs standard RAG.project: Banking FAQ questions mainly need grounded policy retrieval. A graph is justified only when tracing linked accounts, organizational relationships or multiple-hop RCA, and must enforce tenant authorization on every traversal.
Graph RAG vs standard RAG.answer: We chose conventional RAG for policy FAQs because document search was sufficient and simpler to maintain. Graph RAG adds entity and relationship traversal for multi-hop questions, but also increases indexing, security and operational complexity. I would benchmark it against a fixed multi-hop question set before adoption.
workflow: Route multi-hop queries to graph traversal
Combine grounded evidence and verify provenance
mistakes: Claiming graph traversal automatically prevents hallucinations
Ignoring edge-level permissions
Using a graph for simple single-policy lookups
followups: How do you update the graph?
Which query types justify extra complexity?

Edges & conditional edges.simple: A LangGraph workflow is a set of steps connected by paths that decide what happens next.
Edges & conditional edges.technical: Nodes are functions that read/return updates to typed shared state. Edges connect nodes, conditional edges route based on state or classifications, START defines entry, END defines termination. Checkpointers persist graph execution state and thread identifiers associate resumable conversations; looping needs iteration guards.
Edges & conditional edges.example: An intent router selects an FAQ retriever for policy questions and a booking tool for appointment requests.
Edges & conditional edges.project: The banking voice assistant routes recognized speech to a policy Q&A path or verified account/appointment tool, then sends a final answer to TTS.
Edges & conditional edges.answer: In LangGraph, nodes perform work and edges define the flow. Conditional edges select paths based on the state, while the shared state passes messages and validated tool results across nodes. We use checkpointers when conversations must resume, and guard loops with limits to avoid runaway agent execution.
workflow: Conditional edge → RAG or account lookup
mistakes: Putting authorization only in the router prompt
Mutating hidden globals rather than shared state
Omitting terminal/error edges
followups: What is shared state?
When use a subgraph or checkpointer?

Tool calling lifecycle.simple: The model suggests a tool action, but application code decides whether it is safe and actually executes it.
Tool calling lifecycle.technical: LLMs emit structured tool name and arguments against a schema. The orchestrator parses and validates arguments, checks identity/policy, enforces idempotency, calls the backend, records results and returns a sanitized tool message to the model. The model does not gain direct database privileges from the prompt.
Tool calling lifecycle.example: “Book a meeting Friday at 11” becomes a scheduler tool proposal, then a backend slot check and confirmed booking.
Tool calling lifecycle.project: For balance lookup in the banking assistant, caller identity verification and ownership checks must pass server-side before any account data is returned.
Tool calling lifecycle.answer: Tool calling is an orchestrated sequence: the model decides which function is needed, our backend validates the arguments and authorizes the user, executes the operation, then sends the result back for a natural response. Sensitive actions require explicit confirmation and idempotent retries.
workflow: Get user confirmation for side effects
mistakes: Letting model-generated user_id authorize account access
Not distinguishing a proposed call from execution
Retrying payment or booking blindly
followups: What if a tool times out?
How do you stop data leakage between tenants?

Golden dataset (.jsonl).simple: A small set of representative questions and trusted expected evidence/answers used to test changes consistently.
Golden dataset (.jsonl).technical: Golden sets contain sample inputs, relevant sources, expected behaviours and sometimes reference answers/tool calls. Include common, ambiguous, adversarial and negative cases, keep labels versioned and measure evaluator variance. A golden set evaluates quality across regressions; it does not guarantee all production responses.
Golden dataset (.jsonl).example: A question about annual card fees includes the specific policy version and acceptable fee description.
Golden dataset (.jsonl).project: The banking assistant pipeline can block deployment when groundedness drops below the agreed threshold for reviewed banking policy prompts.
Golden dataset (.jsonl).answer: A golden dataset is a versioned collection of representative inputs and expected outputs or evidence. We run a candidate release against it and check groundedness, retrieval, task completion and safety. Failed examples are investigated before releasing, while production traces supply new cases for the set.
workflow: Collect real and synthetic safe examples
Run old and new prompt/model versions
mistakes: Treating LLM-judge score as infallible
Leaking production PII into the dataset
Only testing easy happy paths
followups: How many samples are enough?
What about tools and agent trajectories?

Groundedness.simple: Checks whether the answer is supported by the evidence that was retrieved.
Groundedness.technical: A groundedness evaluator judges consistency between generated claims and provided context, unlike truthfulness against external reality. High groundedness cannot detect a stale or malicious policy document; pair with retrieval quality, source freshness, human review and task success.
Groundedness.example: If context states a fee is ₹500 but the assistant answers ₹700, that numerical claim is ungrounded.
Groundedness.project: For banking FAQs, use context and answer traces from RAG; sample production outputs for automated evaluation and run golden batch gates in CI.
Groundedness.answer: Groundedness measures whether the generated response can be justified by retrieved documents. I test it on a golden dataset in CI and sample traced production answers based on risk, rather than assuming it runs on every single user query. I also monitor context precision, recall and source freshness.
workflow: Capture question, retrieved chunks and answer
mistakes: Calling groundedness the same as factual truth
Ignoring missing evidence and low retrieval recall
Claiming evaluation is free for every response
followups: How is faithfulness different?
Should we sample or score every production answer?

Median & MAD.simple: Use the middle normal runtime and the typical absolute distance from that middle to spot unusual slow jobs.
Median & MAD.technical: Median absolute deviation is median(|x_i−median(x)|), robust against extreme outliers. A robust z-like score can use 0.6745(x−median)/MAD when MAD>0. Add minimum sample thresholds, segmentation by pipeline/load window and special handling for zero MAD.
Median & MAD.example: Durations 10,11,11,12,90 minutes give median 11; mean 26.8 is skewed by the outage.
Median & MAD.project: Your RCA project establishes per-pipeline duration baselines, labels warnings/critical runs and enriches anomalies using Supabase activity logs and dependency metadata.
Median & MAD.answer: We used median and median absolute deviation for pipeline duration anomalies because production runtimes can contain large spikes that distort mean and standard deviation. We calculated robust baselines per comparable pipeline window, classified anomalies and passed correlated logs to an RCA assistant for actionable explanations.
workflow: Compute median and MAD with sample safeguards
mistakes: Claiming MAD is mean absolute deviation
Using one baseline across dissimilar pipelines
Dividing by zero when MAD=0
followups: How do you choose warning thresholds?
How do you address weekly seasonality?

Self-hosted integration runtime.simple: ADF uses a self-hosted integration runtime as a secure worker to reach on-premises or private data systems.
Self-hosted integration runtime.technical: The runtime is a managed Windows agent that executes copy/lookup/connectivity for supported connectors while communicating outbound to Azure control services. Throughput depends on node capacity, concurrent job limits, source/sink constraints and network. Scale out nodes and monitor queues before increasing parallelism.
Self-hosted integration runtime.example: A private SQL Server database can be read by an ADF pipeline without exposing its database port publicly.
Self-hosted integration runtime.project: For enterprise Azure Data Factory pipelines, diagnose concurrency against both self-hosted runtime queueing and backend database pressure.
Self-hosted integration runtime.answer: A self-hosted integration runtime is an ADF execution and connectivity bridge for private or on-premises systems. Concurrent copy activity performance depends on runtime capacity and source throughput; I monitor queued versus running jobs, CPU, memory and network, then scale or tune concurrency cautiously.
workflow: Install and register runtime on secure machine
Monitor job queue and resource use
Scale out or tune pipeline parallelism
mistakes: Assuming concurrent ADF triggers equal concurrent runtime execution
Ignoring source database limits
Opening inbound internet access unnecessarily
followups: How does autoscaling work for SHIR?
What if node is offline?

Azure Speech STT.simple: Speech-to-text converts the caller’s audio into words that the agent can understand.
Azure Speech STT.technical: Streaming recognition consumes correctly framed audio in a supported sample rate/encoding, performs VAD/endpointing, emits interim and final hypotheses, and may use phrase lists or custom speech for vocabulary. Measure word error rate and real-time latency. Authentication must be scoped and secrets stay server-side.
Azure Speech STT.example: An Indian-English caller asks to schedule a financial adviser; the transcript is routed to intent classification.
Azure Speech STT.project: Your banking voice assistant uses Azure Communication Services plus Azure Speech for incoming call transcription, then passes recognized text to a Foundry/LangGraph agent before synthesizing reply audio.
Azure Speech STT.answer: We selected Azure Speech because it integrates with Azure services, supports streaming recognition, configurable language/voice options and operational monitoring. Our application handles sample-rate conversion, turn detection and errors explicitly. We evaluate recognition on domain phrases and track latency, not only LLM answer quality.
mistakes: Confusing audio framing problems with poor LLM reasoning
Hard-coding credentials in the web app
Ignoring speech interruption and final-result timing
followups: Why Azure instead of another STT engine?
How to measure WER and latency?

Speech recognition WER & transcription e.simple: Compare recognized words against a human-correct reference; fewer insertions, deletions and substitutions is better.
Speech recognition WER & transcription e.technical: Word Error Rate = (substitutions + deletions + insertions) / reference word count. Measure by accent, environment, vocabulary and language, then correlate WER with downstream entity/intent accuracy, turn-taking errors and task completion. WER alone does not measure user experience.
Speech recognition WER & transcription e.example: Reference “book an appointment at nine” versus transcript “book appointment at five” can change booking intent despite small overall WER.
Speech recognition WER & transcription e.project: Record consented representative banking test utterances with names/amounts and test Azure Speech recognition separately before tuning downstream agent prompts.
Speech recognition WER & transcription e.answer: I evaluate STT using word error rate on human-transcribed test speech, segmented by noise and accent. But I also test important entities like customer names, balances and appointment times, because one wrong number can be severe even if WER is low.
workflow: Check critical slots and task success
mistakes: Treating a low WER as proof of safe bookings
Using model outputs as the only reference
Ignoring confidence on names and financial figures
followups: What if WER is good but task success is poor?
When use phrase lists?

Supabase RLS vs API authorization.simple: A frontend filter chooses what to display; RLS controls which database rows a user is actually allowed to access.
Supabase RLS vs API authorization.technical: Use auth.uid() ownership predicates on SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE (USING + WITH CHECK), DELETE, and storage.object paths. Keep service-role credentials off browsers; privileged server APIs must validate JWT and resource ownership. Verify cross-user negative tests with separate authenticated sessions.
Supabase RLS vs API authorization.example: Changing `?user_id=someone_else` in a network request must never reveal that person’s uploaded resume.
Supabase RLS vs API authorization.project: Your voice agent/tutor share a Supabase project; Galaxy tables and storage must be separated from call/patient tables and guarded by user-specific policies.
Supabase RLS vs API authorization.answer: Supabase RLS restricts rows inside Postgres according to the authenticated identity, not the user_id sent by the browser. I create explicit policies for every operation, ensure uploads sit in private user-prefixed paths and test two-user isolation. For privileged APIs I still validate JWTs server-side.
workflow: RLS evaluates ownership for each operation
Private storage path enforces same UID
mistakes: Trusting caller-provided user_id
Creating only SELECT policies while writes need UPDATE checks
Using public storage for private resumes
followups: Do views bypass RLS?
How do you test two-user isolation?

Wrong answers after deployment.simple: First work out whether the failure came from retrieving the wrong material, reasoning over it incorrectly, or sending/handling the answer incorrectly.
Wrong answers after deployment.technical: Use correlation traces: input normalization, authentication, index version, retrieval top-k and scores, reranker output, prompt template/model versions, completion metadata, tool arguments/results, guardrail decisions and latency. Reproduce on failing production examples with redacted data and compare to the preceding release.
Wrong answers after deployment.example: An agent answers an outdated overdraft policy due to stale chunks even though the model is functioning correctly.
Wrong answers after deployment.project: For the bank voice assistant, separately investigate STT transcript, FAQ retrieval, policy version, routing, tool output and TTS playback before changing prompt text.
Wrong answers after deployment.answer: When users report wrong answers, I collect redacted traces and reproduce representative failures. I compare the STT transcript, retrieved context, prompt/model version and tool logs against a known-good baseline. Then I patch the specific layer and add the failure to our golden regression suite so it does not recur.
mistakes: Blindly increasing temperature or tweaking prompt
Ignoring source freshness
Skipping authorization and privacy review
followups: What if LLM evaluator passed but users complain?
How would you roll back safely?

Revenue fell last quarter.simple: A useful answer needs both the size of the change and the business drivers behind it.
Revenue fell last quarter.technical: A semantic business agent should use approved metrics definitions, warehouse-access-controlled SQL, decomposition by product/geography/customer, contextual changelogs and analyst notes, and explicit separation of correlation from causation. Deterministic SQL computes revenue deltas; LLM narrates grounded findings.
Revenue fell last quarter.example: Revenue declines 12%; SQL isolates a 20% volume drop in one region, then the agent checks campaign/stockout notes.
Revenue fell last quarter.project: This extends your agentic RCA design: structured metric views plus incident knowledge can explain a trend with evidence rather than guessing from raw tables.
Revenue fell last quarter.answer: I would use a read-only SQL tool over governed metrics, compare this and previous quarters, then drill into price, volume, products and regions. I would join business-event knowledge such as stockouts, validate the findings and let the LLM explain only what the evidence supports.
workflow: Interpret authorized metric and date semantics
mistakes: Letting model generate unrestricted SQL
Calling correlations proven causes
Using inconsistent time windows
followups: What knowledge base complements SQL?
How do you avoid data leaks across customers?

Databricks 27% savings story.simple: Reduce cloud compute cost by choosing right-sized clusters, job-specific resources and more efficient Spark execution.
Databricks 27% savings story.technical: Cost optimization combines capacity planning, ephemeral job clusters, autoscaling bounds, Photon/instance comparisons where relevant, shuffle tuning, partitioning, run-time/DBU telemetry and repeatable before/after baselines. Report savings with workload-normalized comparisons.
Databricks 27% savings story.example: A scheduled large join job does not need to keep a high-cost interactive cluster running all day.
Databricks 27% savings story.project: The earlier V3 interview catalog mentions a 27% Databricks saving, but the supplied resume does not substantiate that figure. Use it only if you can verify it against billing and workload-normalized cost records.
Databricks 27% savings story.answer: To reduce Databricks cost, I would first establish a workload-normalized baseline, then right-size clusters, move scheduled work to job clusters, tune costly Spark operations, and monitor reliability and DBU spend. I would quote a percentage saving only if the measured before-and-after results verify it.
workflow: Move scheduled workloads to right-sized job clusters
mistakes: Claiming 27% only from one configuration tweak
Ignoring data volume drift and job quality
Optimizing cost while missing SLAs
followups: How was 27% measured?
What were the latency trade-offs?

Today's policy document changes.simple: A changed policy must replace stale search evidence before the assistant can answer from the new version.
Today's policy document changes.technical: Publish events trigger parsing/chunking/embedding, metadata and ACL validation, and a version switch. Preserve source timestamps, deactivate previous-version chunk IDs and run retrieval checks before production. Consider cache invalidation, reindexing latency and rollback.
Today's policy document changes.example: A mortgage fee changes on Tuesday: retrieval after publishing must cite Tuesday’s effective document rather than Monday’s cached chunk.
Today's policy document changes.project: For banking voice agents, ingestion and index freshness should be observable independently of the assistant deployment cycle.
Today's policy document changes.answer: When a policy changes I detect the source version, process only the changed document, rebuild its chunks and embeddings, then atomically activate them. I remove or retire stale entries, invalidate caches and run a retrieval regression before saying the new policy is live.
workflow: Switch active index + invalidate stale cache
mistakes: Only updating the original PDF without indexing
Leaving conflicting versions active
Skipping tenant or document authorization
followups: What if update processing fails?
How do you audit effective dates?

Tool-call accuracy & task success.simple: An answer can sound right but still book the wrong appointment; evaluate the actual action.
Tool-call accuracy & task success.technical: Evaluate schema validity, tool selection, required/extra calls, parameter correctness, authorization, idempotency and final task state against deterministic expected outcomes. Use mock tools in CI and sandbox tools in controlled integration tests; log traces for debugging.
Tool-call accuracy & task success.example: For “schedule 2 pm with adviser Jane,” success means a verified 2 pm booking under the right customer, not just a polite confirmation.
Tool-call accuracy & task success.project: In your banking voice assistant, use synthetic account fixtures and mocked scheduler responses to test safe lookup and booking flows end to end.
Tool-call accuracy & task success.answer: I measure tool-call accuracy separately from response quality. We validate the chosen tool, structured arguments, authorization and final backend state against golden test cases. CI uses mocks for reproducible tests and controlled integration runs verify real tool contracts and idempotent behaviour.
workflow: Define expected tool trajectory and final state
Gate failures and add incident cases
mistakes: Scoring only response similarity
Not testing side effects
Confusing tool call requested with tool call completed
followups: How do you handle asynchronous tool errors?
How do you test without exposing real banking data?

Azure AI Evaluation SDK.simple: Run automated checks on a collection of prompts and answers to detect poor quality before release.
Azure AI Evaluation SDK.technical: Azure AI Evaluation offers model-based evaluators and programmatic batch pipelines. Pass evaluator-required fields such as question, response, context and reference, calibrate metrics to release policy and record prompt/model/test dataset versions. An LLM judge score needs human spot-checks.
Azure AI Evaluation SDK.example: Fail a candidate assistant release if average groundedness drops below 4.0/5 on an approved golden dataset.
Azure AI Evaluation SDK.project: Your interview prep emphasized automated groundedness, relevance, coherence and similarity checks integrated into Azure DevOps or GitHub Actions.
Azure AI Evaluation SDK.answer: We use programmatic evaluation to test a versioned golden dataset whenever prompts, models or retrieval change. Groundedness, relevance and coherence tell us different things. We set quality thresholds, inspect failures and maintain human-labeled examples to calibrate judge scores before promoting a release.
workflow: Generate answers for frozen golden examples
Block release and record evaluation artifact
mistakes: Calling coherence proof of factual correctness
Setting arbitrary thresholds without calibration
Measuring averages only and ignoring severe failures
followups: Can you evaluate every production response?
How do you compare with Ragas?
